---
title: "When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Okay. Suppose that we ask whether the duration of an event changes a participant's choice between *in* and *for*. Before choosing a regression model, we should ask what sort of thing the response is. Here it is a choice with two possible values. We record *in* as $1$ and *for* as $0$.

Now consider what a fitted value should mean. For participants and items with a particular set of predictor values, the fitted value should be the probability of an *in* response. A probability must lie between zero and one. Ordinary linear regression does not impose that restriction: its fitted line may continue below zero or above one. This gives us the first reason to generalize the model.

We can see the problem in the [**SuperTelicity**](https://github.com/SuperMereo/supertelicity) cloze data. Each row records one participant's choice after an event description. Participants contribute multiple rows, so the choices from one person may resemble one another even after we supply the predictors.

Recall that a [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) restricts attention to cases with specified predictor values. If $Y=1$ marks an *in* choice, the conditional probability $\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\mathbf x)$ is the proportion we would expect among cases with predictors $\mathbf x$. For a zero--one response, that probability also equals the conditional [expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd), or long-run average, of $Y$. Its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd), which measures spread around that average, changes with the probability. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

A second issue concerns the rows. [Independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) would require learning one response to provide no information about another after we condition on the predictors. Because the same participants and sentences recur, that claim requires additional model structure. We will first isolate the zero--one response problem and return to repeated units when we introduce mixed models.

The prompt supplies an event description followed by a temporal phrase choice. `prep_in=1` means that the participant selected *in*; `prep_in=0` means that the participant selected *for*. `numeral` and `time_unit` record the magnitude selected with that phrase, and `log_duration_minutes` converts it to natural log minutes. The prepared table does not contain the source sentence, so we show an actual nontext row rather than fabricate a stimulus.

```{r}
#| label: load-supertelicity
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(st) == 9160L, all(st$prep_in %in% 0:1))
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
st$duration_centered <- st$log_duration_minutes -
  mean(st$log_duration_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
st_duration <- st[!is.na(st$duration_centered), ]
c(rows = nrow(st), duration_rows = nrow(st_duration),
  participants = length(unique(st$participant_id)),
  sentences = length(unique(st$sentence_id)))
```

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-supertelicity-row
st[1L, c(
  "participant_id", "sentence_id", "verb", "verb_type",
  "contentfulness", "clause_type", "preposition", "prep_in", "numeral",
  "time_unit", "log_duration_minutes"
)]
```

The duration comparison uses only rows with a selected temporal magnitude. Thus it describes `r nrow(st_duration)` of the `r nrow(st)` cloze choices; missing durations keep it from representing the full experiment.

## The support problem in observed data

For $Y_i=1$ when participant $i$ chooses *in* and $Y_i=0$ otherwise,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1\mid\mathbf x_i)=\pi_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

These identities follow directly from the [Bernoulli distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-distribution.qmd). Conditional on the predictors,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]
=0(1-\pi_i)+1(\pi_i)=\pi_i,
$$

and, because $Y_i^2=Y_i$ for a zero--one variable,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]
=\mathbb{E}[Y_i^2\mid\mathbf x_i]-\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]^2
=\pi_i-\pi_i^2.
$$

This is the **support-and-variance problem**: the mean must remain between zero and one, and the conditional variance changes with that mean.

A linear probability model, $\pi_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$, does not constrain $\pi_i$ to $[0,1]$. A logit model instead sets $\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$.

```{r}
#| label: fit-support-models
#| echo: true
lpm <- lm(prep_in ~ duration_centered + verb_type, data = st_duration)
logit_fit <- glm(prep_in ~ duration_centered + verb_type,
                 family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = st_duration)
grid <- expand.grid(
  duration_centered = seq(min(st_duration$duration_centered),
                          max(st_duration$duration_centered), length.out = 201L),
  verb_type = levels(st_duration$verb_type)
)
grid$log_duration_minutes <- grid$duration_centered +
  mean(st$log_duration_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
grid$linear <- predict(lpm, newdata = grid)
grid$logistic <- predict(logit_fit, newdata = grid, type = "response")
breaks <- unique(quantile(st_duration$log_duration_minutes,
                          probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 13L)))
st_duration$duration_bin <- cut(st_duration$log_duration_minutes,
                                breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
binned <- aggregate(cbind(prep_in, log_duration_minutes) ~ duration_bin + verb_type,
                    st_duration, mean)
range(grid$linear)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-support-models
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), color = "grey75", linewidth = .35) +
  geom_point(data = binned,
             aes(log_duration_minutes, prep_in, shape = verb_type), size = 1.7) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(log_duration_minutes, linear, linetype = verb_type),
            color = "grey55", linewidth = .6) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(log_duration_minutes, logistic, linetype = verb_type),
            color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-.4, 1.1)) +
  labs(x = "Selected duration (log minutes)",
       y = "Probability of an in-completion", shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

Points are observed bin proportions; grey lines are linear probability fits; blue lines are logistic fits. The fitted linear means range from `r round(min(grid$linear), 3)` to `r round(max(grid$linear), 3)`, leaving the probability scale. The logistic curves remain inside it.

This is also a variance problem: Bernoulli variance is determined by the mean, rather than by one constant residual variance. A generalized linear model repairs both pieces by choosing a response family with the right support and a link that constrains the mean. These population fits expose that architecture; they do not reproduce the manuscript's Bayesian mixed model or account for repeated participants and sentences.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does binary support motivate a Bernoulli response but not uniquely select the logit link?
2. What population does the duration complete subset omit?
3. Why does a different variance at different fitted probabilities not count as an extra nuisance in a Bernoulli model?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Bernoulli supplies the zero--one sampling distribution. Several one-to-one links, including logit and probit, can map an unconstrained predictor to a probability. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. It omits cloze responses for which no temporal magnitude was retained, so its target is conditional on duration availability. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. The Bernoulli model fixes the conditional variance at $\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ once the mean is specified. The family therefore builds mean-dependent variance into the response distribution; no constant residual variance parameter remains to estimate. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

We now turn to [link functions](link-functions.qmd), which let us build an unrestricted regression equation while keeping its predicted probabilities between zero and one.
